paragraphs: The paper studies optimization problems whose objective is built by nesting several functions inside one another, while the solution must remain in a closed convex constraint set. The algorithm receives noisy function values and gradients. Its analysis assumes that these estimates satisfy specified unbiasedness and second-moment conditions.

The proposed method uses conditional-gradient updates, avoiding projection onto the constraint set and instead using linear minimization. To reach an epsilon-stationary solution, it requires stochastic-oracle calls scaling as epsilon to the power minus two and linear-minimization calls scaling as epsilon to the power minus three. Stationarity is the stated target, rather than a guarantee of finding a global optimum.

The number of nested functions affects hidden constants separately from the accuracy dependence, so adding levels does not change those powers of epsilon. The method is also parameter-free and converges without growing mini-batches. For a single function, the authors additionally establish a high-probability result with only polylogarithmic dependence on inverse confidence, extending the analysis beyond its general complexity bounds.
neurips-2022-a-projection-free-algorithm.tldr: A projection-free method optimizes noisy nested objectives with convergence bounds that separate accuracy requirements from nesting depth.

paragraphs: Neural networks used to solve partial differential equations must satisfy both the equation inside a domain and conditions along its boundary. Training with separate penalties for these requirements can create competition between loss terms. This paper develops a unified way to satisfy boundary conditions automatically, including Dirichlet, Neumann, and Robin conditions in geometrically complex problems.

The approach introduces additional fields borrowed from mixed finite element methods. These fields reformulate the equations so that all three boundary-condition types take equivalent linear forms. The authors then derive analytical general solutions for those conditions and use them to construct the form of the network's candidate solution. Boundary compliance is therefore built into that construction.

This removes the need for extra boundary-condition loss terms and alleviates their competition with the equation loss. The authors also provide a theoretical argument that the additional fields can stabilize training. Experiments on real-world equations with complex geometry demonstrate effectiveness against state-of-the-art baselines, supporting the value of combining analytical constraint handling with neural solution methods.
neurips-2022-a-unified-hard-constraint-f.tldr: The framework builds common boundary conditions directly into neural PDE solutions, reducing competing training losses and potentially stabilizing optimization.

paragraphs: Algorithms with predictions use learned forecasts to improve decisions while seeking worst-case protection when forecasts are unreliable. Much of this research assumes access to one predictor. This paper considers the more practical situation in which several predictors are available and their relative quality cannot easily be determined in advance.

The central challenge is that a collection of predictions brings both opportunity and an identification cost. An algorithm would ideally perform according to the strongest predictor in the collection, but it must somehow determine which predictions deserve attention. Simply having more forecasts does not settle how to use them effectively. The paper makes this selection problem part of algorithm design.

The authors develop algorithms for matching, load balancing, and non-clairvoyant scheduling, and prove performance bounds for each setting. These results extend problems previously studied with a single predictor to prediction portfolios. The contribution is a set of problem-specific methods and guarantees for exploiting multiple forecasts, rather than an unconditional claim that access to more predictors always improves performance.
neurips-2022-algorithms-with-prediction-.tldr: The paper develops algorithms and performance bounds for using multiple predictors while accounting for the cost of identifying useful predictions.

paragraphs: Hierarchical reinforcement learning organizes behavior around intermediate goals, which can help an agent explore when rewards are sparse. The difficult part is discovering useful intermediate goals and their dependencies. This paper argues that relying primarily on randomness during exploration makes that discovery inefficient in complicated environments.

The proposed CDHRL framework uses causal relationships among environment variables to guide construction of a subgoal hierarchy. These relationships provide information about which subgoals are reachable and how achieving one may depend on others. The framework then uses policies for the discovered subgoals to investigate further causal relationships. Hierarchy construction and causal discovery thus support one another through an ongoing learning process.

Experiments in 2D-Minecraft and Eden show that CDHRL discovers high-quality hierarchies and significantly improves exploration efficiency. The stated finding concerns these two complex environments. Its broader methodological significance is the use of causal dependencies to organize exploration: the agent's emerging understanding of the environment helps determine what it should attempt next.
neurips-2022-causality-driven-hierarchic.tldr: CDHRL uses causal dependencies to discover subgoal hierarchies and improves exploration in two complex reinforcement-learning environments.

paragraphs: Abstraction can make reinforcement learning more efficient by representing an environment through a simpler decision process. This paper develops that idea for continuous control, where both states and actions can vary continuously. It extends MDP homomorphisms, mappings that connect an original decision process to an abstract one, to this setting.

The authors derive a policy-gradient theorem for the abstract process. This provides a foundation for optimizing policies while taking advantage of approximate symmetries in the environment. Building on the theorem, they introduce an actor-critic algorithm that learns both the policy and the abstraction mapping simultaneously. A lax bisimulation metric guides this joint learning of representations and behavior.

Experiments on DeepMind Control Suite benchmark tasks demonstrate the method's effectiveness. In particular, using these mappings for representation learning improves performance when observations are pixels. The result links the theoretical abstraction machinery to a practical control problem: learning useful decision-making representations directly from visual observations, alongside learning the actions to take.
neurips-2022-continuous-mdp-homomorphism.tldr: The paper extends MDP abstractions to continuous control and jointly learns abstractions and policies, improving performance from pixel observations.

paragraphs: Algorithmic extrapolation asks whether a model trained on small, simple reasoning problems can handle larger, harder ones. Recurrent systems offer a way to attempt this: repeatedly apply the same computation, allowing more iterations for a difficult instance. The paper identifies a failure of this approach in which behavior deteriorates as the number of iterations grows, calling it overthinking.

The authors introduce two changes aimed at sustaining useful computation. A recall architecture preserves an explicit copy of the original problem in memory, keeping that information available throughout processing. A progressive training routine discourages behavior tied to a particular iteration number and instead encourages operations that can continue to be repeated.

Together, these changes address both retention of the problem and the repeatability of the learned computation. The authors report that they prevent overthinking and enable extremely difficult extrapolation tasks. The finding supports the importance of how recurrent computation is structured and trained when additional iterations are meant to extend reasoning beyond the complexity encountered during training.
neurips-2022-end-to-end-algorithm-synthe.tldr: Preserving the problem in memory and progressively training repeatable computation prevents reported overthinking failures in recurrent reasoning systems.

paragraphs: Experimental design asks which measurements will be most informative about a quantity of interest. This paper studies that question for linear functionals of functions in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, or RKHSs. The target can be a quantity derived from a function, with applications including gradient maps, integrals, and solutions to differential equations.

Classical work in linear regression often assumes an estimability condition that permits unbiased estimation. The authors extend the framework to RKHSs and allow the desired functional to be inferred approximately with a fixed bias. Their algorithms construct designs that explicitly account for this bias, making approximation part of the design problem rather than requiring unbiased recovery.

The paper also derives finite-sample confidence sets for both fixed measurement designs and adaptive ones. These guarantees assume sub-Gaussian noise and certify bounded estimation error with high probability. Together, the design algorithms and confidence sets connect two decisions: where to collect information and how much confidence to place in the resulting approximate estimate.
neurips-2022-experimental-design-for-lin.tldr: The paper designs informative measurements for RKHS functionals while accounting for fixed bias and providing high-probability error guarantees.

paragraphs: This paper examines how a neural network moves through training, rather than only whether its final predictions are accurate. It studies gradient flow, the continuous-time form of gradient-based optimization, for a ReLU network with one hidden layer. The analysis specifically assumes orthogonal input vectors, squared-error loss, and small initialization.

Within this setting, the authors prove that training reaches zero loss despite the nonconvex optimization problem. They also characterize an implicit preference for solutions with minimum variation norm. This connects successful fitting to the type of solution selected by training: reaching a fit and choosing among possible fits are separate aspects of the dynamics.

The analysis further quantifies an early alignment phenomenon and proves that the trajectory follows a particular sequence of movements from saddle to saddle. These results offer a detailed account of intermediate training behavior, not just an endpoint guarantee. Their explanatory scope is the stated shallow-network setting with orthogonal inputs and small initialization.
neurips-2022-gradient-flow-dynamics-of-s.tldr: For shallow ReLU networks with orthogonal inputs and small initialization, the paper characterizes zero-loss convergence, implicit bias, and saddle-to-saddle training dynamics.

paragraphs: Masked image modeling hides image patches during training, but hierarchical vision transformers need mechanisms that can efficiently process the remaining, irregularly distributed patches. This paper enables those models to discard masked patches and compute only on visible ones. Its changes address both window-based attention and convolution layers.

Group Window Attention divides visible patches into equal-sized groups and performs masked attention within each group. This controls attention's quadratic cost as the number of patches grows. A dynamic-programming procedure further improves the grouping to minimize overall attention computation. The method also replaces convolution layers with sparse convolutions that operate on the visible-patch representation.

For examples including Swin and Twins Transformers, the authors report training about 2.7 times faster and reducing GPU memory use by 70%. They report competitive ImageNet classification performance and superior downstream COCO detection results. These findings show that the proposed sparse processing can substantially reduce training resources while retaining strong evaluated performance, with the framework intended to cover most hierarchical vision transformers.
neurips-2022-green-hierarchical-vision-t.tldr: Grouped attention and sparse convolutions let hierarchical vision transformers skip masked patches, substantially reducing training time and memory in reported examples.

paragraphs: GAN training couples two evolving components: a generator and a discriminator. Their joint behavior makes successful convergence and common failures difficult to explain. This paper studies those dynamics in a specific setting where real and generated samples are finite, discrete sets and the discriminator uses a kernel.

The authors introduce an Isolated Points Model that makes these interactions tractable. It assumes that real samples are separated by distances much larger than the kernel width. Consequently, any generated point is influenced by at most one real point. This separation allows the analysis to characterize conditions under which training converges to either desirable or undesirable minima.

The model explains approximate mode collapse and divergence, two distinct ways training can fail. Numerical simulations reproduce these behaviors in line with the analysis. The contribution is therefore a controlled account of how coupled training dynamics produce different outcomes under the isolated-point assumptions, providing more than an observation that GAN optimization can be unstable.
neurips-2022-instability-and-local-minim.tldr: An isolated-point model of GANs with kernel discriminators characterizes convergence conditions and explains approximate mode collapse and divergence.

paragraphs: Predicting a multi-agent system requires accounting for how participants affect one another. Several kinds of interaction can coexist, and their strengths can differ. This paper introduces Interaction Modeling with Multiplex Attention, or IMMA, to represent that layered structure when predicting future behavior.

IMMA uses a latent graph with multiple layers, allowing separate interaction types to be represented independently. Attention accounts for differences in relationship strength. The resulting model combines distinctions about what kind of interaction is present with distinctions about how strongly it matters. The authors also introduce Progressive Layer Training as a training strategy for this architecture.

The reported evaluations cover social navigation, cooperative task achievement, and team sports. Across these scenarios, IMMA outperforms state-of-the-art models in trajectory forecasting and relation inference. The authors also demonstrate that it can improve zero-shot generalization and support examination of how different interactions affect behavior. This makes the representation useful both for forecasting agents' movements and for probing the relationships underlying those predictions.
neurips-2022-interaction-modeling-with-m.tldr: IMMA represents multiple interaction types and strengths to improve multi-agent forecasting, relation inference, and demonstrated zero-shot generalization.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement-learning agents commonly incorporate useful experience into network weights during training. This paper augments that process with context-sensitive database retrieval, letting an agent consult relevant information while producing its outputs. The retrieval mechanism supports the network's own computations and is learned end to end.

A practical consequence is that the agent can attend to newly added information without retraining, simply by expanding the retrieval dataset. The authors investigate the approach in offline reinforcement learning for 9x9 Go. Fast approximate nearest-neighbor methods retrieve relevant examples from tens of millions of expert demonstration states, making consultation of a very large experience collection feasible.

Go's vast state space makes the task depend on generalization beyond exact matches to previous positions. In the reported study, attending to retrieved information significantly improves prediction accuracy and game-play performance compared with using the demonstrations only as training trajectories. The result demonstrates the value of keeping experience available for direct consultation alongside what the network has already learned in its parameters.
neurips-2022-large-scale-retrieval-for-r.tldr: An offline Go agent improves prediction and play by retrieving relevant expert states from a large database during decision-making.

paragraphs: Large neural networks can demand more memory and computation than resource-constrained applications can afford. This paper proposes an algorithm that finds efficient low-rank subnetworks during training. Because the compact representation is maintained as learning proceeds, the intended savings cover training as well as subsequent evaluation.

The central idea is to represent weight matrices through low-rank factors and update those factors directly. The authors constrain the matrices to a low-rank manifold, meaning that training updates must remain within the prescribed class of representations. They derive appropriate updates using techniques from dynamic model order reduction for matrix differential equations.

The algorithm also adjusts matrix ranks automatically during training to meet a desired approximation accuracy. This lets the representation's size adapt as learning proceeds instead of requiring one unchanged rank throughout. Numerical experiments on fully connected and convolutional networks demonstrate efficiency, and the authors report significant reductions in time and memory for both training and evaluation. The contribution combines compact parameterization with a training procedure designed to preserve and adapt that compactness.
neurips-2022-low-rank-lottery-tickets-fi.tldr: The method trains adaptive low-rank network factors directly, reducing reported time and memory costs during both training and evaluation.

paragraphs: Dynamic algorithm configuration uses reinforcement learning to adjust an algorithm's settings as it operates across problem instances. A single configuration policy may struggle when the algorithm has several different types of hyperparameters. This paper proposes dividing that responsibility among cooperating agents, with one agent assigned to each hyperparameter type.

The resulting MA-DAC framework expresses configuration as a contextual multi-agent Markov decision process. A cooperative reinforcement-learning algorithm learns how the agents should act together. This formulation makes the heterogeneity of the settings explicit while retaining a shared configuration task. The authors instantiate it on an established algorithm for multi-objective optimization.

Experiments show better performance than the tested configuration methods based on heuristic rules, multi-armed bandits, and single-agent reinforcement learning. They also demonstrate generalization to different problem classes. These findings support coordinated specialization as a useful approach to configuring complex algorithms. The authors additionally release the environments as a benchmark, allowing the configuration setting to serve as a testbed for multi-agent reinforcement-learning methods.
neurips-2022-multi-agent-dynamic-algorit.tldr: MA-DAC assigns cooperating agents to different hyperparameter types and improves dynamic configuration in the evaluated multi-objective optimization setting.

paragraphs: A graph model trained to predict links may later encounter graphs much larger than those used in training. This paper theoretically studies that size shift for graph message-passing neural networks. The question is whether learned structural representations retain useful information about links as the deployment graph grows.

The authors prove finite-size bounds showing that predictors based on structural embeddings of individual nodes can approach random guessing on increasingly large test graphs. The result is a possible failure of this representation strategy, rather than a statement that every node-based predictor always fails. They then propose a message-passing model that produces structural embeddings for pairs of nodes.

For the pairwise construction, the authors prove bounds showing convergence toward embeddings of a continuous function that preserves out-of-distribution link-prediction ability. Experiments on random graphs agree with the theoretical findings. The contrast identifies representation granularity as consequential: encoding a pair directly can retain predictive structure that individual-node embeddings may lose under increasing graph size.
neurips-2022-ood-link-prediction-general.tldr: The paper shows how node-based link predictors can degrade on larger graphs and develops pairwise embeddings with theoretical generalization guarantees.

paragraphs: Outsourcing training to a cloud server can provide computation that an end device lacks, but uploading local data may be impractical because of sensitivity or bandwidth constraints. This paper proposes using a selected portion of public data as a proxy for the client's data during cloud training.

Efficient Collaborative Open-source Sampling, or ECOS, constructs that proxy through interaction between the cloud and the client. The cloud probes its public dataset to learn about the client's data distribution. Communication consists of a small number of compressed public features and scalar responses from the client. The sampling process is designed to keep both communication and computation efficient while identifying suitable public examples.

Empirical studies report improvements in automated client labeling, model compression, and label outsourcing across several learning scenarios. These findings support the usefulness of tailoring public training data to a client's distribution. The stated mechanism avoids uploading the client dataset while still allowing information from the client to guide which cloud-held examples are used.
neurips-2022-outsourcing-training-withou.tldr: ECOS selects public proxy data for cloud training through efficient client interaction, avoiding upload of the client's dataset.

paragraphs: Lipschitz constraints limit how much a network's outputs can change as its inputs change. Such networks are used in robustness and distribution comparison, but are often regarded as less accurate classifiers. This paper examines that perception and argues that 1-Lipschitz networks have several useful classification properties.

The authors show that these networks can match classical networks in accuracy and fit arbitrarily difficult decision boundaries. They also characterize the most robust classifier under a robustness metric chosen to reflect operational needs, identifying it with the WGAN discriminator. That characterization depends on the chosen metric; it specifies what robustness means for the result.

The paper further establishes favorable generalization under milder assumptions and emphasizes that loss-function hyperparameters control the balance between accuracy and robustness. The practical message is that evaluating a Lipschitz constraint in isolation misses an important part of the learning setup. The loss and its settings influence which balance is obtained, while the theoretical results support the potential for classifiers with provable accuracy and robustness.
neurips-2022-pay-attention-to-your-loss-.tldr: The paper establishes classification advantages of 1-Lipschitz networks and shows that loss hyperparameters are crucial to their accuracy–robustness trade-off.

paragraphs: Score-based generative models perform strongly in applications such as image generation and audio synthesis, but the meaning of their training objective is still being developed theoretically. This paper connects that objective to Wasserstein distance, a measure of discrepancy between the generated distribution and the data distribution.

The precise result is an upper bound: Wasserstein distance is bounded by a constant multiple of the square root of the training objective, plus a fixed offset. Lowering the objective therefore reduces the objective-dependent part of this bound. The fixed offset matters because the theorem does not simply equate the objective with Wasserstein distance or say that zero objective necessarily makes the distance zero.

The proof uses optimal-transport theory, adding another interpretation alongside the previously established connection to Kullback-Leibler divergence. Numerical experiments support the findings. By examining the derived bounds, the authors also propose techniques for tightening them. The contribution gives a mathematical link between score-based training and distributional closeness while retaining the constants and offset that qualify that link.
neurips-2022-score-based-generative-mode.tldr: The paper bounds Wasserstein distance by a scaled square root of the score-model objective plus a fixed offset.

paragraphs: Many datasets contain groups of related variables as well as missing observations. In education, for example, questions belong to topics, but students may not answer every question. Discovering relationships among topics and estimating missing responses are connected challenges. This paper addresses both within one learning approach.

The proposed VISL model jointly infers structure between variable groups and fills missing values. It uses a generative model with a structured latent space and a graph-neural-network architecture, designed to scale to many variables. This makes the grouping of observations part of the representation rather than restricting structure learning to a small set of individual variables with complete data.

The authors evaluate VISL on synthetic, semi-synthetic, and real educational datasets. They report improved accuracy in both missing-value imputation and structure learning compared with popular and recent approaches. The findings support joint modeling as a way to recover useful relationships even when observations are incomplete, with education providing a setting where group-level structure can help identify learning pathways.
neurips-2022-simultaneous-missing-value-.tldr: VISL jointly learns relationships between variable groups and imputes missing values, improving both tasks in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Fictitious play is a learning procedure for strategic interaction. Earlier extensions to discounted stochastic games established convergence in zero-sum and identical-interest settings, but required players to know transition probabilities and stage payoffs exactly. This paper removes that model-knowledge requirement through regularized, model-free learning procedures.

The proposed methods extend smooth fictitious play to stochastic games. Players use regularized best responses while transitions are unknown and payoffs are perturbed at each stage. The authors prove convergence to stationary regularized Nash equilibria for the same two game classes. The regularization is part of the equilibrium target, so the result concerns the modified game rather than an unqualified equilibrium claim for every stochastic game.

The proof combines continuous smooth best-response dynamics with stochastic approximation. In the single-player case, which is an MDP, the procedures globally converge to an optimal stationary policy of the regularized problem. This makes them an alternative to Q-learning in that setting, while connecting single-agent decision-making and multi-player learning within one family of procedures.
neurips-2022-smooth-fictitious-play-in-s.tldr: Model-free smooth fictitious-play procedures converge to stationary regularized equilibria in zero-sum and identical-interest discounted stochastic games.

paragraphs: Behavior cloning trains a policy to imitate an expert on demonstrated trajectories. TaSIL augments that training objective for continuous control by also penalizing differences in higher-order Taylor-series terms of the learned and expert policies. These terms describe aspects of how the policies change around the demonstrated states, extending what the imitation loss asks them to match.

The theoretical guarantee assumes that the expert satisfies a form of incremental input-to-state stability. Under this condition, a small TaSIL-augmented loss on expert trajectories guarantees a small imitation loss on trajectories produced by the learned policy. In the realizable setting, the authors also provide sample-complexity bounds with roughly inverse-demonstration-count scaling, up to logarithmic factors.

Experiments examine how expert robustness relates to the Taylor-expansion order needed by TaSIL. The authors compare behavior cloning, DART, and DAgger with versions augmented by the proposed loss, reporting significant improvements across multiple MuJoCo tasks. The findings connect the local behavior matched during training to performance when the learned controller generates its own experience.
neurips-2022-tasil-taylor-series-imitati.tldr: TaSIL matches higher-order policy behavior to improve imitation, with trajectory guarantees for experts satisfying a stated stability condition.

paragraphs: Simulation-based inference uses learned surrogates to approximate Bayesian inference from computer simulators. A concern is that an estimated posterior can express more certainty than the approximation warrants, risking misleading conclusions. This paper introduces Balanced Neural Ratio Estimation, or BNRE, to make posterior approximations tend toward greater conservatism.

BNRE modifies neural ratio estimation by imposing a balancing condition. With a small simulation budget, this condition increases the uncertainty represented by the posterior approximation. At the same time, the method retains the same Bayes-optimal solution and converges to the exact posterior as the simulation budget increases. Its design therefore addresses limited-data uncertainty without changing that limiting target.

The authors provide theoretical arguments for a tendency toward more conservative approximations than standard NRE. Across all evaluated benchmarks and simulation budgets, they observe conservative posterior surrogates. That empirical breadth supports the approach without making conservatism an unconditional guarantee. The method is also described as straightforward to add to NRE and as introducing no computational overhead.
neurips-2022-towards-reliable-simulation.tldr: BNRE adds a balancing condition that tends to reduce posterior overconfidence while preserving NRE's Bayes-optimal target without computational overhead.

paragraphs: Player evaluation often measures how actions contribute to desirable outcomes such as goals or wins. This paper adds explicit consideration of risk from uncertain game dynamics. It develops a reinforcement-learning framework that represents uncertainty in action values and uses that representation to evaluate players over a season.

The framework distinguishes two sources of uncertainty. Aleatoric uncertainty reflects randomness intrinsic to the game, while epistemic uncertainty reflects the model's limited knowledge about out-of-distribution examples. A distributional Bellman operator and a feature-space density model capture these sources. The resulting Risk-sensitive Game Impact Metric, or RiGIM, conditions player evaluation on a specified confidence level.

The authors evaluate RiGIM using more than nine million play-by-play events from ice hockey and soccer. They report strong correlation with standard success measures together with consistent risk sensitivity. These findings suggest that the metric retains a connection to familiar measures of sporting success while incorporating how uncertain an action's assessed impact is, rather than reporting only its estimated contribution.
neurips-2022-uncertainty-aware-reinforce.tldr: RiGIM evaluates sports players using action-value uncertainty and a chosen confidence level, showing strong success correlations and consistent risk sensitivity.

paragraphs: Circuit design produces several kinds of information, including the netlist describing connectivity and the layout describing geometry. Treating these sources independently can miss useful connections between them. This paper proposes a shared representation that integrates both kinds of information for learning across electronic-design-automation tasks and stages.

The representation, called Circuit Graph, is a heterogeneous graph that combines topological and geometric information. Circuit GNN processes it through message passing that uses vertex features, edge features, and the differences among information types. The aim is a versatile circuit representation that can serve multiple tasks rather than requiring each information source to be handled separately.

Experiments on two representative prediction tasks report state-of-the-art performance in both logic synthesis and global placement stages. For congestion prediction, the method also achieves a tenfold speedup over the state-of-the-art comparison model. These findings support the practical value of combining circuit connectivity and geometry in one graph, with benefits spanning prediction quality and computation time in the evaluated design settings.
neurips-2022-versatile-multi-stage-graph.tldr: Circuit Graph and Circuit GNN combine connectivity and layout information, achieving strong cross-stage prediction results and a reported tenfold congestion-prediction speedup.

paragraphs: Graph kernels compare graphs through their structure. Random-walk kernels were an early approach, later largely displaced by methods based on the Weisfeiler-Leman test. This paper develops a unified view of these families and revisits what walk-based comparisons can express when their definitions and computations are adjusted.

The authors study node-refinement methods based on walks and formally connect them to Morgan's molecule-canonization algorithm and the Weisfeiler-Leman test. They construct node kernels that permit fine-grained, parameterized neighborhood comparisons and can be computed using the kernel trick. These kernels reach Weisfeiler-Leman expressiveness while allowing neighborhoods to be compared without requiring strict matches.

From this framework, the paper shows that modestly modified classical random-walk kernels can match the expressiveness of the Weisfeiler-Leman subtree kernel. Experiments on real-world classification tasks find that walk-based kernels match or exceed Weisfeiler-Leman kernel accuracy. The theoretical and empirical results together challenge the idea that walk-based methods must be a less capable alternative, while highlighting flexibility in how neighborhood similarity is measured.
neurips-2022-weisfeiler-and-leman-go-wal.tldr: Modified random-walk kernels match Weisfeiler-Leman subtree expressiveness while allowing flexible neighborhood comparisons and achieving competitive classification accuracy.
